opus-5.5.text:
So, I think about this in a couple of layers. The first is that coding is the place where we're seeing the fastest progress, and that's not an accident. Code is verifiable: you can run it, you can test it, you get a clear signal about whether it worked. That makes it unusually amenable to the kind of training we do. And it's also the domain closest to the people building these models, so there's a natural feedback loop. We see it internally, where a large and growing fraction of the code is written with heavy model involvement.

The second layer, which I think is the more important one, is what happens when that capability turns back on AI research itself. A lot of AI research is engineering: running experiments, debugging infrastructure, writing kernels, analyzing results. If models can do more and more of that, you start to get a compounding effect where the models help build the next models. I don't think that's a sudden "foom" overnight, but it's a real acceleration, and you can already feel the early edges of it.

Then the question is how that propagates to the rest of the economy, and here I try to be careful, because I think people make mistakes in both directions. One mistake is assuming that because the model is smart, everything changes immediately. The real world has friction. There are regulations, physical bottlenecks, institutions that move slowly, the need to run clinical trials, build factories, get adoption inside large enterprises. Intelligence doesn't dissolve all of that. I've talked about "marginal returns to intelligence," meaning in some domains, adding a lot more intelligence gets you a lot, and in others you hit constraints that intelligence alone can't route around.

But the opposite mistake is thinking that because diffusion is slow, nothing much changes. I think that's wrong too. Even with friction, if you have something like a "country of geniuses in a datacenter," that's going to compress decades of progress in areas like biology, materials, and software into a much shorter period. Software is the first domino because it's the most digital and the most frictionless. After that come the knowledge-work-heavy parts of the economy, and then, more slowly, the parts tied to the physical world.

So my overall picture is: very fast in coding, fast and accelerating in AI research, and then a wave that moves outward through the economy at a speed set less by the models and more by the bottlenecks around them. And I think a big part of our job, as a company and as a society, is figuring out how to get the benefits of that wave while handling the disruption it'll cause, especially for jobs, responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response calls coding the fastest-progressing area and says AI research is accelerating, but it does not describe aspects of AI research as progressing more slowly than coding.

r002.rationale: It says models can help build the next models, creating compounding acceleration, and predicts that progress will spread to areas such as biology and materials.

r003.rationale: It predicts progress will move outward at different speeds, with physical-world areas advancing more slowly; it does not predict convergence toward a common pace.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this in terms of a kind of two-level process. The first level is what's happening inside AI companies themselves. Coding was always going to be the first domain where this really bit, because it's the one where the model's output is closest to the thing the model is made of. The feedback loop is tight. You can verify whether the code works, you can run the tests, you can see whether the experiment produced the result. And over the last couple of years we've gone from models that could autocomplete a function to models that can take a task that would have taken a strong engineer a day or two, go off, and come back with something that's often right. Inside Anthropic now, the large majority of code is written by Claude, and increasingly the models are doing pieces of the research itself: running ablations, reading the results, proposing the next experiment.

So the first thing that happens is that AI research accelerates. Not infinitely, because the bottlenecks move. Compute is a bottleneck. Running experiments takes wall-clock time. Deciding what's actually worth trying still involves taste, and the models are getting better at that too, but it's not instantaneous. But I think it's reasonable to say that the effective number of researchers you have goes up substantially, and that compounds.

Then the second level is the rest of the economy, and here I think people make two opposite mistakes. One group says, well, if it's happening in coding, it'll happen everywhere next month. The other group says coding is special and nothing else will move. I think the truth is that coding is a leading indicator, and the lag to other fields is real but it's measured in a couple of years, not in decades. Biology, materials science, parts of finance, legal work, customer-facing work. These are all domains where the cognitive part of the job can increasingly be done by a model, but where the surrounding structures, the regulation, the physical experiments, the institutional decision-making, move at human speed.

So what I'd expect is something that looks less like a sudden jump in GDP and more like a steadily widening gap between what's technically possible and what's actually been deployed. And the interesting question for the next several years isn't really about the models. It's about how fast the rest of the world can absorb them. That's the thing I think people underestimate on both ends.

r001.rationale: It describes coding as a fast-moving domain, then notes that AI research is accelerating but remains constrained by compute, experiment time, and research judgment.

r002.rationale: It calls coding a leading indicator and predicts that model capabilities will extend to other fields over the next couple of years, including biology, materials science, finance, and legal work.

r003.rationale: It predicts a real lag and gradual deployment across the economy; it does not say that successor-model building will make progress converge to a common pace.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between making intelligence cheaper and making the entire process that uses intelligence faster. Coding is a particularly direct case: you write something, run it, get feedback, and improve it. If AI gets very good at that loop, you can see substantial acceleration.

AI research is especially interesting because improvements can feed back into the systems doing the research. Better models help you build better models. But the strength of that feedback depends on what’s actually limiting progress. If you’re waiting for a training run or for more compute, having more research ideas doesn’t automatically remove that constraint.

And then, across the economy, you encounter different bottlenecks. A biological discovery still needs to be tested. A factory still needs to be built. Organizations have to change how they work. So I wouldn’t expect every sector to accelerate at the same rate just because coding does.

The question I’d focus on is: how much of each process can intelligence accelerate, and how quickly do the remaining steps become the limiting factor? You could have extraordinarily rapid progress in software and AI research alongside a more gradual—but still very consequential—transformation of the physical economy.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as a direct, potentially fast feedback loop, while noting that AI research can be held back by training time or compute even when more ideas are available.

r002.rationale: It describes better models helping build better models, but does not clearly state that faster model development will accelerate AI capabilities in other domains.

r003.rationale: The response says sectors will not accelerate at the same rate and contrasts rapid software and AI progress with a more gradual physical economy transformation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between making the intellectual work faster and making the whole process faster. Coding is particularly amenable to acceleration because you can write something, run it, get feedback, and iterate. A lot of that loop takes place entirely on a computer.

AI research has some of those same properties. If models can help write the code, design experiments, and interpret the results, that could accelerate the development of the next generation of models. But the size of that effect depends on what’s actually limiting progress. You still have to run the experiments, and you still need compute.

Across the broader economy, the constraints are more varied. Imagine that you could do the intellectual part of developing a new drug much faster. You’d still have to manufacture it, test it, and establish that it’s safe and effective. Those steps don’t automatically accelerate at the same rate as coding.

So I’d expect an uneven process. Some digital activities could move very quickly, while other sectors take longer because they depend on physical experiments, investment, or organizational changes. The important question is how much of each process AI can accelerate—and what becomes the next bottleneck once it does.

r001.rationale: It says coding is especially easy to accelerate because its feedback loop is computer based, while AI research still depends on running experiments and having compute, contrasting coding with slower research bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help develop the next generation of models, but does not state that faster model development will accelerate AI capabilities in other domains.

r003.rationale: It predicts uneven progress across the economy, with physical experiments, investment, and organizational changes remaining bottlenecks; it does not predict convergence to a common pace.
